parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: When the growth factor binds its receptor, the receptor changes shape and becomes active (for example, a receptor tyrosine kinase phosphorylates itself). This starts a signal transduction cascade of relay proteins, such as a kinase cascade. The cascade activates transcription factors, which turn on genes for cell-cycle proteins like cyclins and Cdks. The cell then passes the G1 checkpoint and divides.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: (i) Independent variable: growth factor concentration (ng/mL). Dependent variable: mean percent of cells in mitosis after 24 hours. (ii) Any one controlled variable, such as temperature, cell type, culture medium or nutrients, starting cell density, incubation time, or CO2 level. (iii) As growth factor concentration increases, the percent of cells in mitosis rises, from 4.0% at 0 ng/mL to 17.1% at 20 ng/mL. Each step adds less than the one before, so the increase is levelling off.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: (i) Percent change = (17.1 − 4.0)/4.0 × 100 = 13.1/4.0 × 100 = 327.5%, an increase. (ii) The ±2SE range at 5 ng/mL is 8.14 to 10.06. The range at 10 ng/mL is 12.64 to 14.56. The two ranges do not overlap, so the difference between the means is statistically supported.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: The percent of cells in mitosis would fall below 17.1%, probably to near the 0 ng/mL baseline of about 4%. With the receptor blocked, the growth factor cannot bind, so the signaling pathway that drives the cell cycle is not activated, even though plenty of growth factor is present.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: In each generation only the flies with the most extreme heritable phenotype (most bristles) reproduce. Their alleles for high bristle number make up a larger share of the next generation's gene pool. Over repeated generations the frequency of those alleles rises, so the population mean shifts toward more bristles.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: (i) IV: number of generations of selective breeding. DV: number of abdominal bristles per fly. (ii) Temperature, type or amount of food, rearing density, light cycle, or age/sex of the flies counted. (iii) The mean bristle number goes up with more generations, from 34.0 at 0 generations to 52.5 at 9. The increase is small from 0 to 3 and larger after that.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: (i) (52.5 − 34.0)/34.0 × 100 = 18.5/34.0 × 100 ≈ 54.4% increase. (ii) Generation 3: 37.0 ± 2.68 = 34.32–39.68. Generation 6: 45.6 ± 2.76 = 42.84–48.36. The ±2SE intervals do not overlap, so the difference is statistically supported.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: The mean would stay about the same as the starting value, around 34 bristles. With random mating and no selection, flies with high and low bristle numbers reproduce equally. Allele frequencies would not change in any consistent direction, apart from small random drift.
parts.issue: The reference says 'about 35' while the starting mean is 34.0. That is still within the 'close to starting value' range, so it is acceptable.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: As drug concentration goes up, the mean percent of cells in mitosis goes down: 11.9% at 0 µM, 7.0% at 5 µM and 2.4% at 20 µM. It is highest at 0 µM.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: The ±2SE ranges are 11.08–12.72 at 0 µM, 6.40–7.60 at 5 µM and 2.14–2.66 at 20 µM. The 0 µM range does not overlap either of the other ranges, so the data support the claim for both comparisons.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: If the drug stops cells at a checkpoint before mitosis (for example the G2/M or G1/S checkpoint), cells collect in interphase and fewer move on into mitosis. That lowers the percent of cells in mitosis.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: The mean percent of eggs with an abnormal number of chromosomes goes up as the mice get older: 2.0% at 3 months, 9.2% at 12 months and 28.5% at 18 months. The biggest jump comes between 12 and 18 months.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: The ±2SE ranges are 3 months: 1.80–2.20; 12 months: 8.30–10.10; 18 months: 25.12–31.88. The 18-month range does not overlap either of the other ranges, so the data support the claim that the 18-month mean is greater than both of the other means.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: In nondisjunction, homologous chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis I, or sister chromatids fail to separate in meiosis II. As a result, one daughter cell gets an extra chromosome (n+1) and the other is missing one (n−1). If the egg is the cell that keeps the wrong number, it is aneuploid, and fertilizing it gives a trisomic or monosomic zygote.

A plot of ln[A] against t curves (0, −0.788, −1.224, …), and so does [A] against t.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: k increases. At a higher temperature, molecules collide more often, and a larger fraction of the collisions have energy at least equal to the activation energy. More collisions therefore succeed.

parts.your_answer: k increases. At a higher temperature the molecules have more kinetic energy, so they collide more often. More importantly, a larger fraction of collisions have energy at or above the activation energy, so more collisions lead to reaction.

parts.label: (A)
parts.your_answer: The third worker's marginal product is 70 − 52 = 18 chairs. Its marginal revenue product is 18 × $3 = $54.

parts.label: (B)
parts.your_answer: MRP of worker 1 = 30 × $3 = $90. MRP of worker 2 = 22 × $3 = $66. MRP of worker 3 = $54. Workers 1 and 2 each add more than the $55 wage, but worker 3 adds less, so the firm hires 2 workers.

parts.label: (C)
parts.your_answer: Worker 3 adds $54 in revenue but costs $55 in wages. Hiring that worker would lower profit by $1.

parts.label: (D)
parts.your_answer: Demand for labor increases (the curve shifts right). MRP = MP × P, so a higher product price raises MRP at every quantity of labor.

parts.label: (E)
parts.your_answer: Fewer. A monopsonist faces an upward-sloping labor supply curve, so to hire one more worker it must raise the wage for all its workers. That makes its marginal factor cost higher than the wage. It hires where MRP = MFC, which means fewer workers (at a lower wage) than in a competitive labor market.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: A competitive inhibitor has a shape like the substrate's, so it binds to the enzyme's active site. While it is bound, the substrate cannot get in. With fewer active sites free, fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form and less product is made per minute.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: (i) The independent variable is the concentration of compound X (µM). The dependent variable is the initial reaction rate (µmol of product per minute). (ii) Examples to keep constant: temperature, pH, substrate concentration or enzyme concentration. (iii) As the concentration of compound X goes up, the mean initial rate goes down: 40.7, then 28.8, then 20.1, then 11.8 µmol/min.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: (i) Percent change = (11.8 − 40.7) / 40.7 × 100 = −28.9 / 40.7 × 100 ≈ −71.0%, a decrease of about 71%. (ii) At 2 µM the range is 28.8 ± 2.38, or 26.42 to 31.18. At 4 µM the range is 20.1 ± 2.18, or 17.92 to 22.28. These ranges do not overlap, so the difference is statistically supported.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: Compound X would lower the rate less. The rate with the inhibitor would be closer to the rate without it, and at very high substrate it would approach the uninhibited maximum. This is because many more substrate molecules compete with the inhibitor for the active sites, so substrate fills most of them.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: Water potential (Ψ) is the potential energy of water per unit volume. It measures how freely water will move and depends on solute potential and pressure potential (Ψ = Ψs + Ψp). Water moves from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: Plot sucrose molarity (M) on the x-axis (independent variable) and percent change in mass (%) on the y-axis (dependent variable). Scale both axes evenly, with the y-axis running from about -25 to +15. Plot all six points and connect them with a line or line of best fit; the points fall on a straight line with a slope of -32% per M.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: (i) Change in mass is 0 at about 0.35 M, found from 11.2 - 32x = 0, which gives x = 0.35. (ii) Null hypothesis: sucrose molarity has no effect on the percent change in mass of the potato cores.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: In 0.4 M NaCl the cores would lose more mass than in 0.4 M sucrose. A drop of about -14% would be expected, similar to 0.8 M sucrose. NaCl breaks into two ions (i = 2), so the solution has twice as many solute particles. This makes the solute potential (Ψs = -iCRT) more negative and lowers the solution's water potential below that of the potato cells, so more water leaves the cores.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: The bottom template strand. Its left end is 3' and its right end is 5', so the new strand on it runs 5' to 3' from left to right. That means it grows toward the fork as the fork moves right, so it can be made continuously.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the 3' end of a growing strand. On the top template, the new strand has to be made from right to left, away from the fork. Each time the fork opens more template, synthesis has to start again from a new primer, which produces short Okazaki fragments that ligase later joins.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: Reading left to right: 3'-GCGATCTTA-5'. This is the complement of CGCTAGAAT, and it runs antiparallel to the top strand.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: The top template is an original (parental) strand, and it stays base-paired with the newly made complementary strand. Each daughter DNA molecule therefore has one old strand and one new strand, which is what semiconservative replication means.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: The bottom template strand (3' on the left, 5' on the right). The new strand on it runs 5'→3' from left to right, so it grows toward the fork as the fork moves right, which lets it be made continuously.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: DNA polymerase can add nucleotides only to the 3' end of a growing strand, so the new strand runs antiparallel to its template. On the top template, the new strand has to grow leftward, away from the fork. Each time the fork opens up more template, synthesis has to start again near the fork with a new primer. This makes short Okazaki fragments, which are later joined together.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: 3'-CCACCCACCG-5' (left end is 3', right end is 5')

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: The new strand pairs with the original top template strand. The finished double helix therefore has one parent (old) strand and one newly made strand. That is what semiconservative replication means.

parts.label: A
parts.your_answer: A change in the nucleotide sequence (a substitution, insertion or deletion) changes the mRNA codons transcribed from the gene. That can put a different amino acid into the protein, cause a frameshift, or create an early stop codon. A different amino acid sequence can change how the protein folds, so its shape and function can change.

parts.label: B
parts.your_answer: Independent variable: how long the cells are exposed to UV light (0, 10, 20 or 30 s). Dependent variable: the number of colonies (antibiotic-resistant cells) that grow on the antibiotic plates.

parts.label: C
parts.your_answer: The longer the UV exposure, the more colonies will grow on the antibiotic plates. The 0 s plate should have the fewest colonies, or none.

parts.label: D
parts.your_answer: UV light damages DNA (for example, by forming thymine dimers), and errors made while repairing or copying the damaged DNA cause mutations. Longer exposure causes more DNA damage and more mutations. That makes it more likely that some cells get a mutation that makes them resistant to the antibiotic, so more of them survive and form colonies. Since most cells survive these doses, killing by UV does not cancel out this effect.
